title: Saying no — and there are four ways
goal: Learn the one piece of Indonesian grammar where a wrong choice is instantly audible: which word to negate with. Also learn to refuse, decline and apologise the way Indonesians actually do — indirectly.
bekal: say no to an offer without sounding blunt
recognise *nggak*, *gak* and *enggak* as the same word you already know

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Diundang makan malam
dialogs.intro: Rina has invited Sarah to her family's home. Rina's mother, Bu Sri, is making sure her guest is fed.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.text: Sarah, ini bukan makanan pedas. Coba, ya.
lines.id: Sarah, this isn't spicy food. Do try it.
lines.literal: Sarah, this not food spicy. try, yes.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Bu. Wah, enak sekali!
lines.id: Thank you. Wow, this is delicious!
lines.literal: thank you, Mrs. wow, tasty very!

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, sudah kenyang, Bu. Terima kasih.
lines.literal: wow, already full, Mrs. thank you.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.id: Just a little. Don't be shy!

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Baik, sedikit saja. Bu, ini apa? Bukan ayam, ya?
lines.id: All right, just a little. What's this? It isn't chicken, is it?
lines.literal: good, a-little only. Mrs, this what? not chicken, yes?

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.text: Bukan, itu tahu. Sarah tidak makan daging?
lines.id: No, that's tofu. Don't you eat meat?
lines.literal: not, that tofu. Sarah not eat meat?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Makan, tapi saya belum pernah coba tahu.
lines.id: I do, but I've never tried tofu.
lines.literal: eat, but I not-yet ever try tofu.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.id: Now you have! Would you like a drink?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Air putih saja, Bu. Jangan repot-repot.
lines.id: Just water, please. Please don't go to any trouble.
lines.literal: water white only, Mrs. don't trouble-trouble.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.text: Tidak repot. Ini rumah sendiri, ya!
lines.id: It's no trouble. Treat this as your own home!
lines.literal: not trouble. this house own, yes!

notes: **Bukan denies a noun; tidak denies everything else.** Bu Sri says *bukan makanan pedas* (a noun phrase) and *tidak makan daging* (a verb). The rule is mechanical and it never has exceptions, which makes it one of the easiest rules in the book to get permanently right.

**Belum pernah — "not yet ever".** Sarah says she has *never* tried tofu with *belum pernah*, not *tidak pernah*. The difference is real: *belum pernah* leaves the door open ("I haven't, so far"), *tidak pernah* closes it ("I never do"). Indonesian strongly prefers the open door.

**Sudah kenyang is how you decline food.** Saying *tidak mau* to a host would be blunt to the point of rudeness. *Sudah kenyang* ("I'm already full") does the job warmly. Expect to be offered again anyway; being pressed twice is hospitality, not deafness.

**Jangan malu-malu / jangan repot-repot.** Doubling an adjective softens it and makes it into an attitude: *malu* (shy) → *malu-malu* (being shy); *repot* (busy, troubled) → *repot-repot* (going to trouble). These two phrases are exchanged at every Indonesian dinner table.
**Air putih** is literally "white water", and it means plain drinking water. Ask for *air* alone and you may get a puzzled look; ask for *air putih* and you will get exactly what you wanted.

grammars.title: The four negatives
body: Everything hinges on what kind of word comes next.
after: ⚠️ *Saya tidak guru* is the classic foreigner sentence, and it is wrong in a way every Indonesian hears immediately. *Guru* is a noun, so it takes *bukan*. Test yourself with the question "is the next word a thing, or an action/quality?"
*Bukan* on the end of a sentence turns it into a tag question: *Anda orang Australia, bukan?* — "You're Australian, aren't you?" 💬 In speech this becomes *kan*: *Kamu sudah makan, kan?*

grammars.title: Tidak in real speech
body: *Tidak* is written everywhere and said almost nowhere. What you will actually hear:
after: All of them negate exactly what *tidak* negates — the rules do not change, only the sound. *Saya nggak lapar* and *Saya tidak lapar* are the same sentence in two registers.

💬 A very common spoken pattern: the negative goes at the end as a checking tag. *Enak, kan?* — "tasty, isn't it?" And a bare *Nggak apa-apa* (often *gapapa*) means "it's nothing, no problem, never mind", and it is one of the most useful phrases in the language.

blocks.text: Indonesian social life runs on indirectness. A flat *tidak* is grammatically perfect and socially cold, so the language has built a set of soft refusals. Learn these as fixed phrases.

head: Instead of
Say
English
rows: It's not quite right for me.

blocks.text: Notice how often *kurang* ("less, not enough") does the work. Saying something is *kurang enak* rather than *tidak enak* is the difference between "it's not quite to my taste" and "it tastes bad". Indonesians use *kurang* constantly for exactly this reason.

⚠️ And be ready for the same softness coming back at you. *Belum*, *nanti ya*, *mungkin*, *kita lihat nanti* — from an Indonesian these often mean no. Pressing for a definite answer will not produce one; it will only make the conversation uncomfortable.
*Jangan* goes in front of the verb, and the verb stays in its usual shape. That is the whole rule.

*Dilarang* is the official, written version — a passive form you will meet properly in Unit 19. You do not need to produce it, but you should be able to read it on a sign, because that is where it lives.
To soften a *jangan*, add *ya* at the end: *Jangan lupa ya!* This is warm rather than commanding, and it is how friends and family actually speak to each other.

exercises.prompt: Soften the refusal. Write what you would actually say.
items: You are offered a third helping of rice.
A colleague invites you out and you cannot go.
Someone asks a question you do not know the answer to.
A host apologises for the trouble they have gone to.
You want to say the food is not quite to your taste.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: tidak — bukan — tidak — bukan — tidak — bukan
Saya tidak lapar. — Saya bukan guru. — Saya belum makan. — Jangan lupa! — Saya belum pernah ke Bali. — Tidak apa-apa. — Tidak ada kamar.
Sudah kenyang, terima kasih. — Maaf, saya ada acara. — Kurang tahu, Pak. — Jangan repot-repot. — Kurang cocok untuk saya.
Saya bukan guru. — Saya belum makan. — Jangan lupa! — Ini bukan makanan pedas. — Tidak apa-apa.
